subject: Computing

unit.unitOverview:
Welcome to Unit 4, the final unit of Year 6. In this unit you become a computer detective. You will look at a computer from the outside and from the inside, and you will finally understand what all the parts are for, why some computers cost more than others, and how a computer stores your photos, songs and schoolwork as nothing more than 1s and 0s.

A computer system is made of two things working together: hardware (the physical parts you can touch, like the keyboard and the screen) and software (the programs and code, which you cannot touch). Every phone, laptop, tablet and games console is a computer system. By the end of the unit you will be able to choose the right hardware and software for a job, understand the difference between two kinds of programming, explain how data is stored and measured, describe what is inside the case, and discuss how robots are used in industry, including right here in East Africa.

There are five parts to this unit, and it is best to work through them in order because each one builds on the last. First you will learn to select hardware and software (4.1). Then you will compare two ways of writing programs in different programming environments (4.2). Next you will discover how computers store data as binary and how we measure it (4.3). After that you will look inside a computer at the processor and memory (4.4). Finally, you will explore robots in industry (4.5) and design a robot for a real local task.

concepts.title: Selecting Hardware and Software
concepts.explanation:
Hardware and software: what is the difference?

Every computer uses hardware and software together. Hardware is all of the physical parts of a digital device — the parts you can pick up and touch. A keyboard, a mouse, a screen, a hard drive and a games controller are all hardware.

Software is the range of programs you can run on a device. You cannot touch software; it is made of code stored on the computer. Software usually has to be installed before you can use it. Some software is very simple, like the tiny program inside a microwave oven. Some software is very complex, like a big video game or word processing software. Complex software needs better hardware to run smoothly — for example, a large game may need a faster processor and more RAM.

Here is the simplest way to tell them apart: if you can touch it, it is hardware; if it is a program made of code, it is software. A screen is hardware; the game showing on the screen is software.

Each physical part and each piece of software is called a component — an individual part of a larger device. A train is made of components too: a door, a seat and a window are all components of a train. In a computer, each component affects how the machine runs and how it looks. Here are the main hardware components you should know:

Software components let the computer carry out the tasks we want. Word processing software lets us type letters; presentation software lets us make slideshows. Here are common types, with a free or open-source example of each so the Hargeisa lab can keep its costs low:

When you choose hardware or software you weigh up several things at once. There are six factors to think about. A good choice usually balances all of them, rather than being the very best at only one.

Functionality is the range of tasks a device can do. An oven that can roast, grill and bake has high functionality; an oven that can only roast has low functionality. A computer that can do many tasks has high functionality. You can change functionality by adding or removing components.

Aesthetics means how something looks. People like different things — some want a plain black case, some want a see-through case with colourful lights, some want brushed metal. A keyboard that lights up does the same job as a plain one, but some people are happy to pay more because they prefer how it looks.

Speed is how quickly a computer can process data. Three components matter most here. The processor does the thinking; a faster processor loads and runs software more quickly. RAM holds what is being used right now; more RAM lets the computer do more tasks at the same time. Storage holds your files; faster storage lets the computer fetch data more quickly. An ordinary school or office computer does not need a really fast processor, but a computer editing large videos does.

Longevity is how long something stays useful. Shoes that last three years have greater longevity than shoes that last one year. Software is fairly easy to upgrade — a free update can make a computer useful for longer. Hardware is harder to upgrade; often you must buy a new part. Higher longevity usually costs more up front because the parts are better quality.

Cost is how much you pay. The total cost of a computer depends on the cost of each component, plus any software you must buy. Some software is freeware (free), and some costs money. This is why the Hargeisa lab will use free tools like LibreOffice and GIMP wherever possible.

Fit for purpose ties everything together. Something is fit for purpose if it can do the job we want. Would you drive to school in a tractor, or take a caravan on holiday using a bicycle? Of course not — those are not fit for purpose. In the same way, the right computer depends on the person using it.

Freeware is software you do not have to pay for. It often does everything a person needs for simple tasks. Paid-for software usually has extra features, better functionality, and sometimes help support and regular updates that give it more longevity. Compare two photo editors:
concepts.example: For the Hargeisa lab, GIMP is the smart choice: it is free, it runs the media club's tasks well, and the money saved can buy more computers for more students. The lesson is not 'free is always best' or 'expensive is always best' — the lesson is to pick what is fit for purpose for the least sensible cost.

concepts.title: Cost against speed, aesthetics and longevity
concepts.explanation:
As with many things in life, faster usually costs more. When you post a parcel you can pay extra for it to arrive sooner; a faster processor or more RAM costs more money too. But beware: buying only one expensive component may not make the whole computer faster. A very fast, costly graphics card will not make typing a letter any quicker — although it will help a lot if you edit videos.

Attractive devices often cost more. A brightly coloured phone usually costs more than a plain grey one. And higher longevity usually costs more up front but can save money over time. Look at Teacher Nadia comparing two processors for a lab computer:

The standard processor costs $50 less today. But the faster one lasts five years, so it works out at only $40 per year instead of $50 per year. Because it lasts longer, the faster processor actually costs less over time. If Teacher Nadia can afford it now, the faster processor is the better buy.
concepts.example: It is estimated that the world throws away around 50 million tonnes of electronic waste every year. That is a huge amount of metal and plastic. When we upgrade a computer we often throw the old parts away, which can cause pollution. Choosing hardware with good longevity, and recycling old technology instead of dumping it, is kinder to the environment.

concepts.title: Programming Environments
concepts.explanation:
Programming languages and environments

A programming language is a way of writing commands to create a program that tells a computer what to do. There are many programming languages, and different ones are designed for different jobs. Some are best for making games; some are best for writing software like word processors; some exist just for maths; some were made just to build web pages.

We write a programming language (also called code) inside a programming environment. A programming environment is a set of tools for writing and testing programs. One important tool is an editor, where you type your commands. Programming environments are also called development environments. The 'Create' screen in Scratch is a programming environment; so is a Python editor like Thonny.

Learning to program is a bit like learning a foreign language. You can say 'Hello!' in Somali, Swahili and English — the idea is the same, but you write it differently in each language. In the same way, most programming languages let you use the same ideas (like repeating something, or making a decision), but you write them in different ways.

Block-based programming languages

A block-based programming language lets you drag and drop coloured blocks of code with the mouse. The blocks 'click' together like puzzle pieces to build larger sections of code. The most famous block-based language is Scratch, which you used earlier in the course.

In Scratch, blocks that do similar jobs share a colour — for example, all the blocks that move a sprite are the same colour. This makes blocks easy to find, and because you drag them, you never have to remember exactly how to spell a command. That is why block-based languages are often used to teach new programmers, and why they are great for making simple games, animations and music quickly. Here is what a short Scratch program looks like written out as words — remember, you build this by dragging blocks, not by typing:

Block-based (Scratch), shown as words — you build it by dragging blocks

Block-based languages have limits, though. They are not suitable for building large, complicated games, or professional software like a full word processor.

Text-based programming languages

A text-based programming language uses commands you type on the keyboard. Everything must be typed into a file before the program can run. This is very different from dragging blocks. Text-based languages can be harder to learn, because you must remember the commands, know what each one does, and spell them correctly. If you make a spelling mistake, the program will not work. It also takes longer to make fun things happen — a dancing cat that takes a minute to build in Scratch takes much longer to code as text.

So why use them? Because text-based languages are far more powerful. They can build advanced, challenging programs and let you use many different techniques. Almost every piece of software you use was written in a text-based language. A popular example is Python. Here is a Python program that prints the numbers 1 to 10 — the same idea as a common first Scratch project, but typed as text:

And here is Python saying 'Hello!' ten times, so you can compare it directly with the Scratch blocks above. Notice how the command print must be spelled exactly right, and the line below for must be indented (pushed in with spaces):

Other well-known text-based languages include C# (say 'C sharp') and C++ (say 'C plus plus'), which are very popular for writing computer games.

The right choice depends on the job. Use this comparison to decide:

For the Hargeisa coding club, the answer is clear: start with Scratch (block-based) so beginners can build working programs and enjoy quick success, then move on to Python (text-based) once they are ready for bigger challenges. A simple spelling quiz or a rocket-dodging-asteroids game is perfect for Scratch; a professional drawing program with hundreds of tools must be built in a text-based language.

No one knows exactly how many programming languages exist in the world — there are thousands, and new ones are still being created. Amazingly, some languages invented back in the 1950s are still used today. And the software that controls a robot explorer on Mars runs to millions of lines of code!

concepts.title: Storing Data
concepts.explanation:
Two kinds of data: digital and analogue

There are two types of data: digital and analogue. Digital data is made of binary digits — only the numbers 0 and 1. You can think of 0 as electricity switched off and 1 as electricity switched on. Because a computer is full of tiny switches, it understands data made of 0s and 1s perfectly.

Analogue data is different. It is not limited to 0 and 1 — it is a smooth, continuous signal that can take any value, like a wave of light or sound. Something that is continuous keeps going without breaks, and on a graph it draws a smooth curving line. Humans and animals sense the world in analogue. The most common analogue data is sound: your ears hear as sound waves, which are vibrations travelling through the air. Your friends talking, traffic in the city, music from a radio — all of it reaches you as analogue sound waves.

concepts.title: On/off switches become the binary digits 1 and 0
concepts.explanation:
Digitising: turning analogue into digital

To change analogue data into digital data, we digitise it. To digitise sound we use a microphone: the microphone detects the analogue sound waves, and a computer program turns them into digital data (numbers) that the computer can store and use. Computers can digitise other analogue things too, using different sensors — for example, sensors that detect heat or light.

Once data is digital, you can do a lot with it. You can store it on a drive, share it over the internet, and change it with programs. An audio editing program (like the free tool Audacity) can make a recording louder or quieter, add more sound, or delete parts of it — all by changing the digital numbers.

There are laws that protect most music, films and pictures from being copied and shared without permission. It is also simply fair: we respect what belongs to others. Always check that you are allowed to copy or send something before you do.

Because everything is stored as bits, we need a way to measure how much data there is. A single binary number (0 or 1) is called a bit — short for 'binary digit'. It is the smallest unit of storage. Bits are grouped into larger units, and each unit has a name. In this course, as in your textbook, each big unit is 1000 times the one before it.

Notice the two simple rules hidden in that table. To go from bytes to bits, multiply by 8 (because 1 byte = 8 bits). To climb one step up the ladder — bytes to KB, KB to MB, MB to GB, GB to TB — multiply by 1000. To go back down the ladder, divide by 1000. Learning the order bit, nibble, byte, KB, MB, GB, TB by heart makes every storage question easy.

Different sizes suit different jobs. Small files are measured in KB and MB — a photo might be 5 MB. Storage devices like hard drives and USB sticks are measured in GB. Huge storage, like the servers that hold web pages, is measured in TB. Here is roughly what fits into different devices:

RAM is measured in GB. A modern computer often has 8 GB, 16 GB or 32 GB of RAM. RAM comes in smaller sizes than a hard drive because it is faster and more expensive to make.

SSDs (solid state drives) are fast secondary storage, commonly 1 TB, 2 TB or 4 TB.

HDDs (older hard disk drives) can hold a great deal — up to about 22 TB.

USB flash drives and memory cards are small so they fit in a pocket; common sizes are 128 GB and 256 GB.

One terabyte is an enormous amount. Roughly speaking, 1 TB could store about 250,000 songs, or around 1,000 hours of video, or roughly 85 million pages of text. So when Leila's tablet runs out of space for photos, adding a 4 TB SSD would give her room for many years of pictures.

You could store over 17,000 hours of music on just 1 terabyte of storage. If you played it without ever stopping, that is more than 700 days of music — almost two whole years of listening!

concepts.title: Inside a Computer
concepts.explanation:
The processor in a computer is called the central processing unit, or CPU for short. Without the processor, a computer could not process data at all, which is why many people call the CPU the brain of the computer. Most CPUs are tiny — only about 2 square centimetres — yet they are made of many, many small parts.

The most important of those parts is the transistor. A transistor is a tiny device that controls the flow of electricity, rather like a microscopic switch. By connecting huge numbers of transistors together, the CPU can carry out calculations. Modern CPUs contain well over a billion transistors, and the most advanced ones have many billions — all packed into that fingernail-sized chip.

How fast is a CPU? Its speed is measured in gigahertz (GHz). A single hertz means 'one cycle per second', which we can think of as one simple calculation per second. A gigahertz is one billion hertz. So a CPU running at 1 GHz can perform about one billion calculations every second, and a 3 GHz CPU can do about three billion. This number of calculations per second is called the clock speed.

A CPU is far faster than a human at sums, which is why we use computers for very hard calculations. Working out the path of a planet around the Sun by hand would take an extremely long time, but a computer can do it in moments.

A modern CPU can contain well over a billion transistors. Lined up as people, a billion is more than twice the population of the whole European Union — all working together inside a chip smaller than a postage stamp.

A computer needs somewhere to keep data. Computer systems usually have two kinds of storage, and knowing the difference is one of the most important ideas in this unit.

Primary storage is short-term and extremely fast. It usually loses its data when the power is turned off, which is why it is also called volatile storage. The main example is RAM (random access memory). RAM holds all the data and programs the computer is using right now. When you close a program or switch off, that working memory is cleared.

Secondary storage is long-term. It keeps its data even when the computer is turned off, so it is also called persistent storage (the data persists — it keeps on existing). Secondary storage is where we keep programs and files we want to save. A common example is an SSD (solid state drive); hard drives and USB sticks are secondary storage too.

Why does the CPU need fast primary storage right beside it? Because the CPU makes billions of calculations every second, and it must be fed data just as fast. Primary storage costs more per gigabyte because it is made of high-quality materials that let the CPU reach the data almost instantly. Secondary storage is much cheaper and can hold enormous amounts, but it is slower to reach. This is the clearest comparison:

Most computer systems need both. Primary storage gives the CPU the speed it needs to work; secondary storage gives you the space to keep your files safe for later. Phones, laptops, desktop computers and even smart watches all use both kinds of storage together.

concepts.title: Robots in Industry
concepts.explanation:
A robot is a machine that we can program to carry out instructions by itself. When a robot works without help from humans, we say it is autonomous. Making a robot autonomous is difficult: to complete tasks on its own, a robot runs long, complex programs that take programmers a long time to write.

Robots are used a great deal in industry. Industry means work that involves making or selling goods or services. A big part of industry is manufacturing — making large numbers of goods in factories using machines. Car factories and food factories both use many robots.

We often imagine that all robots look like people, but most robots do not look like us at all. They come in many shapes and sizes for many different jobs. Some are a simple robotic arm that lifts a box off a shelf. Some are large, twisting arms that weld cars together. Some are so small and accurate that they connect the tiny circuits inside electronic devices. Some even look like dogs and walk on four legs.

Robots or humans? Advantages and disadvantages

Robots and humans each have strengths and weaknesses, so factories often use both together. Study this comparison carefully:

Robots in car manufacturing and warehouses

Building cars can be dangerous, because engines and doors are very heavy, and every part must be fitted accurately so the car is safe. To make as many cars as possible, factories run through the day and often the night. Robots are perfect for this: they lift heavy parts humans cannot, they weld and measure with great accuracy, and they never need to rest. Yet there are still jobs robots cannot do well — fitting the thin electrical wires inside a car is too fiddly for a robot, so a human does it, because human hands are better at pushing small wires through small holes.

Large online shops use robots too. In huge warehouses, robots drive themselves around, collect the ordered items, and bring them to a place where they are packed and sent to the customer.

Robots in food and farming — close to home

Think how much food the world eats every day. Robots in food factories help produce it quickly. Because robots measure so accurately, they can fill hundreds of containers a minute, each with exactly the same amount. Robots can even harvest some crops automatically.

This is where Uncle Tariq's date farm comes in. In the Gulf and in parts of East Africa, large farms already use machines and robots to sort dates by size and quality, to remove stones and dust, and to pack the dates into boxes at high speed. A sorting robot uses a camera and sensors to check each date, then a robotic arm or gate moves it to the right box. For Uncle Tariq this could mean cleaner, more even packing and far faster work during the busy harvest — a real advantage when the whole crop ripens at once.

But the disadvantages matter too. A sorting robot is expensive to buy and could be hard to repair far from a big city. It can only sort dates the way it is programmed to, so a human is still needed to judge unusual cases, to care for the trees, and to handle anything the machine was not built for. The best answer for a small farm is often a mix: let a machine do the fast, repetitive sorting, and let skilled people do the parts that need judgement and care. Coffee farms in Ethiopia and busy ports like Berbera and Mombasa face exactly the same choice when they think about using robots.

Robots — Humans

Advantages — Work all day and night with no breaks; very accurate; do not need to be paid; can work in dangerous places (for example underwater) · Work well in teams and can change jobs easily; can spot problems a robot would miss; need no complex program; are great at creative and caring tasks

I can explain the difference between a block-based and a text-based programming language.
I can identify when a block-based or a text-based language should be used.
I can explain why data must be changed into numbers (digitised) before a computer can process it.
I can identify the units of storage used to show how large a storage device is, from a bit up to a TB.
I can explain what a computer processor is and describe what it does.
I can identify primary storage and secondary storage in a computer and discuss the role of each.
I can explain what it means for a robot to be autonomous.
